newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: U.S. in balancing act on nuclear trade with China.
newsitem.headline: U.S. in balancing act on nuclear trade with China.

text.p: U.S. moves to relax some curbs on peaceful nuclear cooperation with China highlight the balancing act being performed by American policymakers towards Beijing.

Arms control advocates say the gesture, made by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher this week, is premature and ignores China's history of selling nuclear technology, missiles and other weaponry to states like Iran and Pakistan.
A report in Thursday's Washington Times newspaper, citing the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency, may bolster that argument.

It claims China recently sold Iran missile technology, advanced radar components and nearly 400 tons of chemicals used to produce nerve agents. Transferring missile-guidance components to Iran may violate Beijing's 1994 commitment to curb such sales, the newspaper said.

Reacting to the report in Washington, State Department deputy spokesman Glyn Davies told reporters: "We believe at this stage that, in fact, the Chinese are operating within the assurances they have given us...We've not seen any reason to question their behaviour."

This is consistent with what officials travelling with Christopher have said privately. Some believe stories like the one in the Washington Times are an effort by some government employees to undermine a new policy of engagement with China.
To encourage future cooperation, Beijing must be persuaded good deeds are rewarded and it is possible to meet U.S. and international non-proliferation standards, Christopher's officials argued.
Besides, they added, China has a huge demand for nuclear power reactors and U.S. firms like Westinghouse must not be shut out of that lucrative market.

Calculating multi-billion-dollar profits versus principles and national security is central to U.S. thinking as officials chart what they envision will be a steady new course for broad Sino-American cooperation into the next century.
It includes a push to better manage differences over contentious issues like missile and nuclear technology sales.

After day-long talks in Beijing on Wednesday, Christopher said Washington might let American firms sell minor amounts of nuclear technology to China for peaceful uses before a long- stalled 1985 bilateral agreement is fully implemented.

This could mean allowing cooperation with China -- within months -- in nuclear safety and reactor development. But "big ticket items" like nuclear power reactors themselves still could not be sold until the pact was completely in effect.
The accord allows the sale of U.S.-made nuclear technology for peaceful uses. But it stalled over concerns about China's nuclear sales to countries like Iran and Pakistan.
The U.S. president must first certify China is not providing nuclear assistance to non-nuclear weapons states with unsafeguarded facilities -- which successive administrations refused to do.
Senior U.S. officials said Clinton is still unable to make this certification and it may be some time before he can.

But China has met some U.S. certification requirements and another step was taken when Beijing promised to adopt nationwide export controls. No specific plan for action was given. But officials say the commitment itself is significant.

Chinese leaders last May escaped U.S. sanctions over the sale of nuclear-related ring magnets to Pakistan, arguing they were unaware of the $70,000 deal carried out by one of the communist regime's many arms and technology enterprises.
U.S. officials say if Beijing implements a nationwide export control system, this will reduce destabilising sales and deprive China's leaders of an excuse if any occur.
In the meantime, Christopher said the administration might allow some peaceful nuclear cooperation "consistent with U.S. law" -- which greatly limits what can be done at this time.
Despite such caveats, American arms control expert Gary Milhollin said the U.S. move was a mistake.

"Under long-standing U.S. policy, (peaceful) nuclear trade with the United States is a reward for good behaviour, not a reward for promises only," and China has a history of breaking promises, he told Reuters in a telephone interview.

"The State Department has a pattern of ignoring the evidence," Milhollin said. But even some non-State Department officials with access to classified data say there has been a positive trend in China's efforts to curb proliferation.
After his Beijing talks, Christopher publicly acknowleded that much work remained to be done with Beijing and cited cooperation with Iran as a continuing concern.

But he said China had reaffirmed its commitment to a 1994 agreement not to sell missiles and agreed to seek ratification of an international convention outlawing chemical weapons by the end of April 1997.
